title: Metals: Classification, Sources & Properties
description: Classification of ferrous, non-ferrous metals and alloys; ore extraction; physical and mechanical properties.
content_html:
Classifying Metals

Metals are one of the most versatile material families available to designers. At GCSE level they are divided into three broad groups: ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals, and alloys. Understanding this classification is the starting point for selecting the right material for any product.

Ferrous metals contain iron as their principal element. The iron content makes most of them magnetic and gives them a tendency to rust when exposed to moisture and oxygen. The most common ferrous metals encountered in GCSE Design & Technology are:

  • Cast iron — very hard and brittle, excellent compressive strength; used for engine blocks and heavy machine bases.
  • Mild steel — low carbon content (0.1–0.3%); tough, ductile and easy to weld; the most widely used engineering metal, found in car bodies, structural beams and sheet-metal products.
  • Medium carbon steel — 0.3–0.6% carbon; stronger and harder than mild steel but less ductile; used in axles, crankshafts and railway track.
  • High carbon steel — 0.6–1.4% carbon; very hard but brittle; used for cutting tools, springs and piano wire.
  • Stainless steel — iron alloyed with at least 10.5% chromium; resists corrosion because a thin oxide layer forms on the surface; used in kitchen sinks, cutlery and surgical instruments.
  • High-speed steel (HSS) — contains tungsten, chromium and vanadium; retains its hardness at high temperatures; used for drill bits and lathe cutting tools.
  • High-tensile steel — alloyed to achieve exceptional tensile strength; used in suspension bridges, pre-stressed concrete and aircraft undercarriages.

Non-Ferrous Metals

Non-ferrous metals contain little or no iron. They do not rust (though some corrode in other ways), they are generally non-magnetic, and many have lower densities than steel. Key non-ferrous metals include:

  • Aluminium — low density (2.7 g/cm³), good corrosion resistance, excellent conductor; used in aircraft structures, drink cans and window frames.
  • Copper — excellent electrical and thermal conductor; malleable and ductile; used in electrical wiring, water pipes and printed circuit boards.
  • Zinc — low melting point, good corrosion resistance; mainly used to galvanise steel (coating it to prevent rust) and in die casting.
  • Tin — soft, low melting point, very good corrosion resistance; used to coat steel food cans (‘tin cans’) and as a component of solder.

Alloys are mixtures of two or more elements where at least one is a metal, engineered to combine the best properties of their constituents. Brass (copper + zinc) is harder and more workable than pure copper and resists corrosion well; it is used for taps, door handles and musical instruments. Duralumin (aluminium + copper + magnesium) is far stronger than pure aluminium while remaining lightweight, making it essential in aerospace.

Key Fact

Increasing the carbon content of steel increases its hardness but reduces its ductility. Mild steel has around 0.1–0.3% carbon and is highly ductile; high carbon steel has up to 1.4% carbon, making it hard and brittle. Adding alloying elements such as chromium produces stainless steel, which resists corrosion through a self-forming oxide layer.

Sources: Metals from Ores

All primary metals are extracted from ores — naturally occurring mineral deposits found in the Earth’s crust. Iron ore (haematite) is smelted with coke and limestone in a blast furnace to produce pig iron, which is then refined into steel. Aluminium is extracted from bauxite by electrolysis, a far more energy-intensive process. Because ores take millions of years to form, metals are a finite, non-renewable resource. At current extraction rates, reserves of some metals such as indium and gallium are projected to be depleted within decades.

Mining causes significant ecological damage: open-cast mining strips away topsoil and destroys habitats; tailings (waste rock) can leach heavy metals into waterways; smelting releases carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide, contributing to climate change and acid rain. Socially, mining operations in lower-income countries are sometimes associated with poor working conditions, child labour and community displacement. These concerns form part of the lifecycle assessment of any metal product. Designers can reduce this footprint by specifying recycled metals wherever possible — recycled aluminium uses only 5% of the energy needed to smelt virgin aluminium from bauxite.

For exam questions on sustainability and metals, you should be able to link the finite nature of ores to the importance of recycling, and identify specific ecological harms of extraction (habitat loss, water pollution, carbon emissions) rather than giving vague answers about “harming the environment”.

Physical and Mechanical Properties

When selecting a metal, designers consider two categories of property. Physical properties describe how a material behaves without forces being applied:

  • Melting point — the temperature at which the solid becomes liquid. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal (3,422 °C); tin melts at only 232 °C. High melting points are required for furnace components; low melting points enable die casting.
  • Thermal conductivity — how readily heat passes through the material. Copper and aluminium are excellent thermal conductors; stainless steel is a poorer conductor, which is why it is used for saucepan handles when the body is copper.
  • Electrical conductivity — copper has the highest electrical conductivity of commonly used metals, making it the standard choice for wiring. Aluminium is used where weight matters (overhead power cables).
  • Density — mass per unit volume (g/cm³). Aluminium (2.7 g/cm³) is about one-third the density of steel (7.85 g/cm³), making it preferable where weight reduction is critical.

Mechanical properties describe how a material responds to applied forces:

  • Tensile strength — resistance to being pulled apart. High-tensile steel cables support suspension bridges precisely because of this property.
  • Toughness — the ability to absorb impact energy without fracturing. Mild steel is tough; cast iron is not — it shatters under impact.
  • Malleability — the ability to be shaped by compression (hammering, rolling) without cracking. Gold and lead are the most malleable metals; copper and aluminium are also highly malleable.
  • Ductility — the ability to be drawn out into a wire without breaking. Copper’s excellent ductility is central to its use in electrical wiring.
  • Hardness — resistance to surface scratching or indentation. High carbon steel and HSS are very hard; this is why they are used for cutting tools that must scratch or cut other materials.
Key Fact

Malleability and ductility are frequently confused. Malleability is the ability to be shaped by compressive force (hammering or rolling); ductility is the ability to be drawn into a wire by tensile force. A metal can be malleable without being very ductile — lead is highly malleable but only moderately ductile.

Pure metals often have a single outstanding property but fall short in others — pure aluminium is lightweight and corrosion-resistant but lacks the strength needed for structural applications. By adding small amounts of other elements, designers can engineer an alloy that combines the best qualities of its constituents: duralumin (aluminium + copper + magnesium) achieves tensile strength close to mild steel while retaining aluminium’s low density, making it the material of choice for aircraft frames. This engineering flexibility is why alloys dominate modern manufacturing far more than pure metals.
exam_tip_html: For any question asking you to “justify your choice of metal”, structure your answer as: name the metal → state the relevant property → link it to the function of the product. For example: “Mild steel is suitable because it has high toughness, meaning it can absorb impact without fracturing, which is important for a car body panel that must withstand minor collisions.” Vague answers such as “it is strong” will not score full marks without a named property definition and an application.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ferrous metals contain iron (and are usually magnetic and prone to rust); non-ferrous metals do not; alloys are engineered mixtures designed to combine the best properties of two or more elements.
  • All metals are extracted from finite ores; extraction causes habitat destruction, water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, making recycling and responsible sourcing essential.
  • Physical properties (melting point, conductivity, density) and mechanical properties (tensile strength, toughness, malleability, ductility, hardness) together determine which metal is appropriate for a given product.

glossary_terms.definition: Metals that contain iron as their main element; generally magnetic and prone to corrosion unless treated.
Metals that do not contain iron as a significant element; generally non-magnetic and more resistant to corrosion than ferrous metals.
Naturally occurring rock from which metal can be profitably extracted; a finite, non-renewable resource.
The ability of a material to withstand a pulling (tensile) force without breaking.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following metals is classified as ferrous?
A) Aluminium
B) Copper
C) Mild steel
D) Zinc
Name two physical properties of metals that a designer would consider when selecting a material for electrical wiring.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: electrical conductivity / thermal conductivity / density / melting point. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between malleability and ductility.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Malleability is the ability of a metal to be shaped by compressive forces such as hammering or rolling without cracking.
• Ductility is the ability of a metal to be drawn out into a wire by a tensile (pulling) force without breaking.
• A metal can be malleable without being highly ductile; for example, lead is very malleable but only moderately ductile, whereas copper is both highly malleable and highly ductile. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why aluminium is preferred over mild steel for the manufacture of aircraft body panels.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Aluminium has a much lower density (approx. 2.7 g/cm³) compared to mild steel (approx. 7.85 g/cm³), significantly reducing the overall mass of the aircraft.
• A lower mass reduces fuel consumption and increases payload capacity, both of which are critical for commercial aircraft operation.
• Aluminium forms a natural oxide layer that provides good corrosion resistance without additional coatings, reducing maintenance costs.
• Despite its lower density, aluminium alloys (e.g. duralumin) can achieve sufficient tensile strength for structural applications.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the ecological and social impacts of extracting metals from the Earth’s crust, and discuss how designers can reduce these impacts in their material choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Ecological impacts: open-cast mining removes topsoil and destroys habitats; tailings and leachate pollute waterways with heavy metals; smelting releases CO₂ and SO₂, contributing to climate change and acid rain.
Social impacts: mining communities in lower-income countries may face poor working conditions, health hazards from dust and toxic chemicals, and community displacement.
Designer responses: specifying recycled metals where possible (recycled aluminium uses only 5% of the energy of virgin smelting); choosing metals from certified ethical supply chains; designing for disassembly so metals can be recovered at end of life; minimising material waste through efficient cutting plans.
[6 marks — Mastering: Balanced, developed coverage of both ecological and social impacts plus at least two specific designer responses linked to named metals. Secure: Two impacts and one designer response with some development. Developing: One impact and one response, limited development. Emerging: Vague reference to environmental harm without specific examples.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using stainless steel compared with mild steel for the manufacture of kitchen cutlery.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of stainless steel:
• Contains at least 10.5% chromium, which forms a self-repairing oxide layer, making it highly resistant to corrosion from food acids and washing.
• Hygienic surface that does not react with food; important for food safety.
• Aesthetically appealing; retains a polished appearance over many years without surface treatments.
• Hard and maintains a sharp edge on knives.
Disadvantages of stainless steel:
• Significantly more expensive than mild steel due to the alloying elements (chromium, nickel) and more complex refining.
• More difficult to machine and form than mild steel; harder on tooling, increasing manufacturing cost.
• Poorer thermal conductivity than mild steel (relevant if cutlery is heated, though less critical than for cookware).
• Mild steel is cheaper to purchase, easier to machine and weld, but would require plating or coating to prevent rust, adding cost and potential delamination issues.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion, at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with reference to specific properties and manufacturing considerations. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or superficial response.]

flashcard_questions.q: What makes a metal classified as ferrous?
flashcard_questions.a: It contains iron as its main element and is usually magnetic.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the carbon content range of mild steel?
flashcard_questions.a: 0.1 to 0.3%, giving it toughness and ductility.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does stainless steel resist corrosion?
flashcard_questions.a: At least 10.5% chromium forms a self-repairing oxide layer on the surface.
A mixture of two or more elements where at least one is a metal, engineered for improved properties.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one use of brass and state its two constituent metals.
flashcard_questions.a: Door handles or taps; brass is copper and zinc.
Naturally occurring rock from which metal can be profitably extracted; a finite resource.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does increasing carbon content in steel reduce ductility?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher carbon content makes the steel harder and more brittle, so it fractures rather than deforms.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between malleability and ductility?
flashcard_questions.a: Malleability is shaping by compression; ductility is drawing into wire by tension.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is copper used for electrical wiring?
flashcard_questions.a: It has the highest electrical conductivity of commonly used metals and is highly ductile.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is aluminium preferred over steel for aircraft panels?
flashcard_questions.a: Its density is approximately one-third that of steel, greatly reducing aircraft mass.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one ecological harm caused by mining metal ores.
flashcard_questions.a: Open-cast mining destroys habitats and topsoil.

flashcard_questions.q: Recycled aluminium uses what fraction of the energy of virgin smelting?
flashcard_questions.a: Only about 5% of the energy needed to smelt aluminium from bauxite.
